name: A Simple Task
description: Count the total number of simple cycles (no repeated vertices/edges) in an undirected graph with n <= 19 vertices.
why_hard: Requires bitmask DP over (current vertex set, current endpoint) with careful overcounting correction to avoid double-counting each cycle in both directions and from every starting vertex.

name: Elongated Matrix
description: Reorder the n <= 16 rows of an n x m matrix (traversed column-by-column) to maximize the minimum absolute difference between consecutive visited values.
why_hard: Combines binary search on the answer with bitmask DP over row permutations, a classic "clever state compression" pattern (TSP-style transition costs between rows).

name: Increasing Subsequence II
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Count the number of strictly increasing subsequences of an array, counting subsequences with equal values at different positions separately.
why_hard: A genuine LIS-family generalization — moves from "find the longest" to "count all," requiring a Fenwick tree over compressed values to sum DP contributions in O(n log n).

name: Russian Doll Envelopes
description: Given (width, height) envelope pairs, find the maximum number that can be nested inside each other (both dimensions must strictly increase).
why_hard: A 2D LIS in disguise — needs a sort-then-LIS reduction (with a subtlety in tie-breaking on the sort key) to hit O(n log n).

name: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
description: Given jobs with start time, end time, and profit, schedule a non-overlapping subset that maximizes total profit.
why_hard: Classic weighted interval scheduling DP that requires sorting by end time plus binary search for the last compatible job to reach an efficient solution.

name: Super Egg Drop
description: With k eggs and n floors, find the minimum number of egg-drop trials in the worst case to determine the critical floor.
why_hard: The naive DP is O(kn^2); the intended solution flips the DP state to "moves needed to distinguish m floors with k eggs," an unintuitive reformulation that gets it to O(kn) or O(k log n).

name: The least round way
description: Find a top-left to bottom-right path (moving only right/down) through an n x n matrix that minimizes the number of trailing zeros in the product of visited cells, and output the path.
why_hard: Trailing zeros depend on min(count of factor 2, count of factor 5) along the path, forcing a two-state grid DP plus special-case handling whenever the path is forced through a zero cell.

name: Grid Paths I
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Count the number of paths (moving only right/down) from the top-left to bottom-right of an n x n grid (n up to 1000) that avoid trap cells, modulo 1e9+7.
why_hard: Straightforward recurrence but at n=1000 requires an efficient O(n^2) implementation with careful obstacle handling, a step up from the introductory grid-path DP.

name: Dungeon Game
description: A knight must traverse a grid of damage/heal values from top-left to bottom-right; find the minimum starting health needed so health never drops to zero.
why_hard: The DP must be computed backward from the destination because the natural forward state (max health so far) is not well-defined — a classic "reverse the direction of the DP" trick.

name: Unique Paths III
description: Count the number of paths from a start to an end square in a grid with obstacles that visit every non-obstacle square exactly once.
why_hard: Requires Hamiltonian-path counting rather than simple monotone-path DP, typically solved with bitmask-augmented backtracking/DP over visited cells since paths can move in all four directions.

name: Cherry Pickup
description: Starting from the top-left of a grid with cherries and obstacles, go to the bottom-right and back to the top-left, collecting the maximum cherries (each cell's cherry collected only once).
why_hard: The round trip is modeled as two agents walking forward simultaneously, requiring a 3D state (two positions constrained to the same step count) instead of a naive two-pass DP.

name: Cherry Pickup II
description: Two robots start at the top corners of a grid and move downward simultaneously, collecting the maximum total cherries, sharing cells but each counted once.
why_hard: A genuine multi-agent grid DP — state is (row, col1, col2), and transitions must handle the case where both robots land on the same cell.

name: Round Subset
description: Choose exactly k numbers from a list of n (n <= 200) to maximize the number of trailing zeros in their product.
why_hard: A genuinely multi-dimensional knapsack — state is (items chosen, total factors of 5), tracking the best achievable count of factors of 2 for each state, since trailing zeros are min(#2s, #5s).

name: Knapsack
description: With 8 item weight-classes (1..8), each available in a huge bounded quantity, and a knapsack capacity up to 1e18, find the maximum total weight that fits.
why_hard: Astronomical capacity and counts rule out a direct DP table; it forces recognizing that only a small residue/threshold region needs real DP while the rest is handled by bounded-copy reasoning.

name: Two Sets II
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Count the number of ways to partition {1, ..., n} into two sets with equal sum.
why_hard: A subset-sum counting knapsack where the target sum and array size both scale with n, requiring care with the modulus and the sum/2 target derivation.

name: Elevator Rides
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Given n people (n <= 20) with weights and an elevator weight limit, find the minimum number of elevator rides needed to move everyone up.
why_hard: This is bin-packing dressed as knapsack — the standard solution is a bitmask DP over subsets tracking (rides used, current ride's remaining capacity), an NP-hard-flavored problem tamed only by the small n.

name: Profitable Schemes
description: Choose a subset of crimes (each with a member cost and a profit) using at most n members total that yields profit at least minProfit; count the number of such schemes.
why_hard: A 2D bounded knapsack (members used x profit achieved) where profit must be capped/clamped at minProfit to keep the state space polynomial.

name: Tallest Billboard
description: Given steel rod lengths, split them into two groups (welded end-to-end) whose totals are equal, maximizing that common total.
why_hard: The natural knapsack state isn't a target sum but the running difference between the two sides, requiring a hash-map-indexed DP keyed by signed height difference.

name: Coloring Brackets
description: Given a valid bracket sequence, count the ways to color each character red/blue/uncolored so that exactly one bracket of each matched pair is colored and no two adjacent characters share a color.
why_hard: Classic interval DP over matched bracket ranges with an extra boundary-color dimension in the state to enforce the adjacency constraint across sub-interval joins.

name: Zuma
description: Given a sequence of colored gems (n <= 500), remove contiguous palindromic substrings one at a time to clear the whole sequence in as few operations as possible.
why_hard: The transition must consider merging a middle segment's removal with matching endpoints, an interval DP recurrence subtler than plain palindrome partitioning (dp[i][j] depends on dp over interior splits plus matched-endpoint cases).

name: Removal Game
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Two players alternately remove the first or last number of a list, each maximizing their own score; compute the first player's optimal score.
why_hard: A minimax interval game DP — dp[i][j] must reason about the opponent's optimal response, not just a single maximizer, which is a genuinely different flavor from standard interval optimization.

name: Rectangle Cutting
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Given an a x b rectangle, repeatedly cut a rectangle into two integer-sided rectangles until only squares remain; find the minimum number of cuts.
why_hard: A 2D generalization of matrix-chain-style interval DP — dp[a][b] tries every horizontal and vertical cut position, mirroring the "try every split point" recurrence of classic interval DP but over a 2D dimension space.

name: Burst Balloons
description: Given n balloons with values, burst them one at a time (gaining left*balloon*right coins) to maximize total coins collected.
why_hard: The textbook example of "think about the last event in the interval, not the first" — dp[i][j] represents the best score for bursting everything strictly between i and j last, requiring padding with sentinel 1s.

name: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
description: Given piles of stones in a row, merge exactly k consecutive piles into one at a time (cost = sum merged) until one pile remains; find the minimum total cost, or -1 if impossible.
why_hard: A true generalization of matrix chain multiplication to groups of size k, needing an extra DP dimension for "number of piles currently merged into a group" and a feasibility check based on (n-1) % (k-1).

name: Regular Expression Matching
description: Implement regex matching with support for '.' (any character) and '*' (zero or more of the preceding element) to determine if a pattern matches an entire string.
why_hard: The '*' operator creates non-local transitions (it can match zero occurrences, forcing a skip-back in the DP), making the 2D state transition genuinely tricky to get right.

name: Wildcard Matching
description: Implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' (any single character) and '*' (any sequence, including empty) against an entire input string.
why_hard: Naive O(nm) memoized DP is correct but the interesting challenge is recognizing the greedy two-pointer O(1)-space alternative, making it a good "DP vs. greedy trade-off" problem.

name: Distinct Subsequences
description: Count the number of distinct ways string t appears as a subsequence of string s.
why_hard: The counting recurrence (sum over "use this match" and "skip it" branches) is easy to state but easy to get subtly wrong on the base cases and overflow of counts.

name: Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome
description: Find the minimum number of character insertions needed to turn a given string into a palindrome.
why_hard: A hard palindrome-DP variant that reduces to n - LCS(s, reverse(s)), requiring the non-obvious insight to connect interval palindrome DP with a longest-common-subsequence reformulation.

name: Edit Distance
difficulty: CSES (harder end of the Dynamic Programming section)
description: Compute the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and replacements to transform one string into another.
why_hard: The canonical 2D string-alignment DP; a solid checkpoint before tackling the pattern-matching and constrained variants (wildcard/regex) above.

name: Subsequences (hard version)
description: Given a string of length up to 100 and a target count k (up to 1e12), repeatedly add distinct subsequences to a set at cost (n - length); find the minimum total cost to reach k distinct subsequences.
why_hard: Requires counting distinct subsequences of each length via DP (not just total distinct subsequences), then greedily consuming the cheapest (longest) ones first — a layered combination of counting-DP and greedy selection.

name: Kefa and Dishes
subtopic: Bitmask DP (traveling salesman / Hamiltonian path style, assignment problem, broken-profile/tiling DP)
description: Choose an ordered sequence of at most m dishes (no repeats) maximizing total satisfaction plus bonuses for specific adjacent-dish pairs.
why_hard: Classic Hamiltonian-path-flavored bitmask DP over "set of dishes eaten so far, last dish eaten" with up to 18 dishes.

name: Vladik and cards
subtopic: Bitmask DP (traveling salesman / Hamiltonian path style, assignment problem, broken-profile/tiling DP)
description: Given up to 1000 cards each with a value 1-8, choose the longest subsequence that can be split into 8 non-decreasing subsequences (one per value).
why_hard: Requires binary-searching the answer length, then an assignment-style bitmask DP over "last used position for each of the 8 values" combined with greedy/binary-search reasoning — a genuinely tricky state design.

name: Counting Tilings
subtopic: Bitmask DP (traveling salesman / Hamiltonian path style, assignment problem, broken-profile/tiling DP)
description: Count the number of ways to tile an n×m grid completely using 1×2 tiles (horizontal or vertical).
why_hard: The canonical broken-profile bitmask DP — process the grid cell by cell, carrying a bitmask of which cells in the current "profile" are already filled.

name: Elevator Rides
subtopic: Bitmask DP (traveling salesman / Hamiltonian path style, assignment problem, broken-profile/tiling DP)
description: Partition n people (each with a weight) into the minimum number of elevator rides, each ride capacity-limited.
why_hard: Classic "partition into minimum-cost groups" bitmask DP over subsets (dp[mask] = min rides, extra weight used in current ride), similar in spirit to bin-packing/TSP subset DP.

name: Maximum Students Taking Exam
subtopic: Bitmask DP (traveling salesman / Hamiltonian path style, assignment problem, broken-profile/tiling DP)
description: Seat the maximum number of students in a classroom grid with broken seats so no student can see an adjacent-row/diagonal neighbor's answers.
why_hard: Row-by-row broken-profile-style bitmask DP where each row's mask must be internally valid (no two adjacent bits) and compatible with the previous row's mask (no diagonal conflicts) — two layers of bitmask compatibility checking.

name: The Fair Nut and the Best Path
subtopic: Tree DP (max independent set on tree, tree diameter via DP, rerooting technique)
description: Given a tree with vertex weights, find the maximum weight of a simple path (sum of vertex weights along it).
why_hard: Direct generalization of tree-diameter-via-DP: at each node combine the best two "downward chains" from children while handling negative contributions correctly.

name: Work Group
subtopic: Tree DP (max independent set on tree, tree diameter via DP, rerooting technique)
description: On a tree where each employee has a rating, pick a subset of nodes with no supervisor-subordinate pair included, maximizing total rating minus a fixed penalty per chosen member.
why_hard: Weighted maximum-independent-set-on-a-tree DP with the added twist of deciding per-subtree whether including the root subtree's answer beats zero, requiring careful combination of children's dp states.

name: Tree with Maximum Cost
subtopic: Tree DP (max independent set on tree, tree diameter via DP, rerooting technique)
description: For every possible choice of root, compute sum over all vertices of (vertex value × distance to root), and output the maximum over all roots.
why_hard: Textbook rerooting technique — compute the answer once via one DFS, then re-derive every other root's answer in O(1) via a second DFS that transfers subtree contributions.

name: Binary Tree Cameras
subtopic: Tree DP (max independent set on tree, tree diameter via DP, rerooting technique)
description: Place the minimum number of cameras on tree nodes (each covers itself, its parent, and its children) so every node is monitored.
why_hard: Requires a 3-state tree DP (node has camera / node is covered without a camera / node is uncovered) with a subtle greedy-DP hybrid argument for correctness — a step up from plain max-independent-set DP.

name: Beautiful numbers
subtopic: Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property up to N)
description: Count integers in [l, r] that are divisible by the sum of their own digits.
why_hard: The archetypal hard digit DP: since the divisor (digit sum) varies, you must DP over (position, remainder mod LCM(1..9), digit-sum-so-far, tight-flag), forcing a clever LCM-based state compression.

name: Magic Numbers
subtopic: Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property up to N)
description: Count numbers in [l, r] built by concatenating the substrings "1", "14", and "144" in some order.
why_hard: Requires designing a custom finite automaton over digit positions to track partial matches of "1"/"14"/"144", then running digit DP over that automaton's states.

name: Segment Sum
subtopic: Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property up to N)
description: Compute the sum of all integers in [l, r] that contain at most k distinct decimal digits.
why_hard: Standard digit-DP counting is not enough — you must simultaneously track a bitmask of digits used and accumulate the actual sum contribution of each digit position, combining digit DP with careful combinatorial bookkeeping.

name: Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set
subtopic: Digit DP (counting numbers with a digit property up to N)
description: Given a set of allowed digits, count how many positive integers ≤ N can be formed using only those digits (repetition allowed).
why_hard: A clean, from-scratch introduction to the "process digits of N one position at a time, branch at the first strictly-smaller digit" digit DP pattern, including the tricky same-length-as-N edge case.

name: Gargari and Permutations
subtopic: DP on DAGs (longest/shortest path in a DAG, counting paths)
description: Given k permutations of 1..n, find the longest common subsequence that appears (as a subsequence) in all k permutations simultaneously.
why_hard: Reduces multi-permutation LCS to longest-path-in-a-DAG DP, where an edge (u, v) exists only if u appears before v in every one of the k permutations.

name: Toss a Coin to Your Graph...
subtopic: DP on DAGs (longest/shortest path in a DAG, counting paths)
description: Binary search on a value x, keep only edges whose weight is ≥ x, and find the longest path (in number of edges) achievable in the resulting graph, restricted to a length budget k.
why_hard: Combines binary search on the answer with a longest-path-in-DAG DP over a graph that must first be shown to be acyclic (or detected as having a long-enough cycle) for the chosen threshold.

name: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
subtopic: DP on DAGs (longest/shortest path in a DAG, counting paths)
description: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing path of adjacent cells in a matrix.
why_hard: The grid's "increasing value" edges implicitly define a DAG; the intended solution is memoized DFS (longest path in a DAG) rather than naive exponential search.

name: Largest Color Value in a Directed Graph
subtopic: DP on DAGs (longest/shortest path in a DAG, counting paths)
description: In a directed graph where each node has a color, find the largest possible count of any single color along a path, or report that a cycle makes the answer undefined.
why_hard: Requires topological-sort-driven DP carrying a full 26-color frequency vector per node while simultaneously detecting non-DAG (cyclic) input.

name: Removal Game
description: Two players alternately remove a number from either end of an array trying to maximize their own total; both play optimally — find the first player's best possible score.
why_hard: The canonical interval minimax DP: dp[i][j] represents the best score difference achievable on subarray [i, j], built from two overlapping smaller subproblems.

name: Stick Game
description: Two players alternately remove sticks from a pile using only a given set of allowed move sizes; determine who wins with optimal play for every pile size up to n.
why_hard: A textbook win/lose-state DP (Grundy-style) over pile sizes, where each state's outcome depends on reachable smaller states — must be computed for all sizes up to n efficiently.

name: Letter Picking
description: Two players alternately remove a letter from either end of a string, each trying to end up with the lexicographically better multiset of removed letters after optimal play from both sides.
why_hard: Interval minimax DP with a three-way outcome (win/lose/draw) per state and a non-obvious per-state comparison rule between the two players' objectives.

name: Stone Game III
description: Two players alternately take 1, 2, or 3 stones from the front of a pile, each trying to maximize their own score; determine who wins (or if it's a tie) with optimal play.
why_hard: Requires a suffix minimax DP tracking score differential with a branching factor of 3 per state and a careful sign-flip argument to translate "maximize my score" into a single recurrence.

name: Fish
description: n fish (n ≤ 18) swim in a pond; on each step two random fish meet and one eats the other with a given probability — compute, for every fish, the probability it survives to be the last one.
why_hard: Combines a bitmask DP over "which fish are still alive" with probability transitions and a clever trick (fixing the encounter order) to make the state space tractable.

name: Bad Luck Island
description: On an island with rocks, scissors, and paper creatures that randomly meet and eliminate each other Rock-Paper-Scissors style, compute the probability each species survives.
why_hard: A 3-dimensional probability DP over (rocks remaining, scissors remaining, paper remaining) where each state's probability flows into three possible next states — a clean example of expected-outcome DP over compound state.

name: New Year and Arbitrary Arrangement
description: Given probabilities of typing characters 'a' or 'b' at random (and a target k), compute the expected number of occurrences of the substring "ab" in a string built until k copies of "ab" appear (with a length cap).
why_hard: Requires setting up an expected-value recurrence over (count of 'a's so far, count of "ab" substrings so far) and reasoning carefully about linearity of expectation combined with an early-stopping condition.

name: Dice Probability
description: Compute the probability that the sum of n dice rolls (each showing 1..6) lands in a given range [a, b].
why_hard: Foundational probability DP — dp[i][s] = probability the sum after i dice is s — that scales naturally into harder biased-dice and weighted variants.

name: Inversion Probability
description: Given n elements each independently and uniformly assigned one of two possible values (with per-position choices), compute the expected number of inversions.
why_hard: Uses linearity of expectation over all O(n²) pairs combined with a running-DP aggregate (expected number of "smaller" elements seen so far) to avoid the naive quadratic blow-up.

name: Ciel and Gondolas
subtopic: DP optimization techniques (monotonic deque optimization, divide & conquer optimization, Knuth's optimization, convex hull trick)
description: Partition n people standing in a line into exactly k contiguous, non-empty groups to minimize total "unhappiness" (sum over each group of a pairwise-cost function).
why_hard: The quintessential divide-and-conquer optimization (and alternatively Knuth's optimization) problem — the naive O(n²k) DP is reduced to O(nk log n) by proving the optimal split point is monotonic in the DP layer.

name: Yet Another Minimization Problem
subtopic: DP optimization techniques (monotonic deque optimization, divide & conquer optimization, Knuth's optimization, convex hull trick)
description: Split an array into exactly k contiguous segments minimizing the sum, over segments, of C(count of each value in the segment, 2).
why_hard: A second core divide-and-conquer optimization exercise, this time requiring an efficient two-pointer/BIT-maintained cost function as the split point recurses — combining D&C optimization with incremental cost maintenance.

name: The Bakery
subtopic: DP optimization techniques (monotonic deque optimization, divide & conquer optimization, Knuth's optimization, convex hull trick)
description: Split an array of shop types into exactly k contiguous "zones" to maximize the total number of distinct shop types across all zones.
why_hard: Requires combining divide-and-conquer optimization on the DP layer with a segment-tree-maintained "distinct count" cost function that must be recomputed as the split boundary moves.

name: Watching Fireworks is Fun
subtopic: DP optimization techniques (monotonic deque optimization, divide & conquer optimization, Knuth's optimization, convex hull trick)
description: You move along a line of positions over time to maximize happiness gained from fireworks launched at given times/positions/values, with a per-second movement speed limit.
why_hard: The DP transition at each time step is a sliding-window maximum over a range that shifts predictably, making it a direct application of monotonic-deque DP optimization to bring an O(n·d²) DP down to O(n·d).

name: Kalila and Dimna in the Logging Industry
subtopic: DP optimization techniques (monotonic deque optimization, divide & conquer optimization, Knuth's optimization, convex hull trick)
description: Cut down n trees (each requiring a specific axe strength and giving specific value if the previous tree cut used a weaker or equal axe) to maximize total value, minimizing total axe cost.
why_hard: One of the most commonly cited introductory convex hull trick problems — the DP transition is a min-plus query over lines, and lines are inserted in an order that permits the simple monotonic CHT (no need for Li Chao tree).

name: Subsequences
subtopic: DP combined with data structures (e.g. LIS in O(n log n), DP + Fenwick tree)
description: Given n points (x, y), find the maximum length of a sequence of points chosen in increasing order of x and non-decreasing order of y (a 2D "staircase" subsequence).
why_hard: A direct 2D generalization of the O(n log n) LIS trick — requires a Fenwick tree keyed on the y-coordinate (after coordinate compression) to query "best dp value among all smaller-or-equal y so far" in O(log n).

name: Increasing Subsequence II
subtopic: DP combined with data structures (e.g. LIS in O(n log n), DP + Fenwick tree)
description: Count the number of strictly increasing subsequences ending at each position of an array (not just the longest one).
why_hard: Extends the classic O(n log n) LIS-length trick to counting: a Fenwick tree over compressed values must maintain running sums of subsequence counts rather than just a running maximum.

name: Russian Doll Envelopes
subtopic: DP combined with data structures (e.g. LIS in O(n log n), DP + Fenwick tree)
description: Given (width, height) pairs of envelopes, find the maximum number that can be nested inside each other (each dimension must strictly increase).
why_hard: Reduces a 2D nesting problem to 1D LIS via a sort-then-patience-sorting trick (sort by width ascending, height descending for ties) so the O(n log n) LIS algorithm applies directly — a subtle but standard reduction.

name: Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids
subtopic: DP combined with data structures (e.g. LIS in O(n log n), DP + Fenwick tree)
description: Given cuboid dimensions (each freely rotatable), stack cuboids on top of each other (each dimension of the one on top must be ≤ the one below) to maximize total height.
why_hard: A 3D generalization of the LIS/patience-sorting family — requires normalizing each cuboid's dimensions, sorting, then running an O(n²) or O(n log n) longest-chain DP, testing whether the LIS-style reduction insight transfers to three dimensions.
